### Regulatory

**[MEM] med confidence — have Egyptian counsel confirm all of this:**
- **Egypt has no dedicated franchise statute.** No franchise-disclosure-document regime equivalent to a US FDD, and no mandatory pre-sale registration.
- Franchising is governed by general contract law, the **Commercial Trade Law No. 17 of 1999** (which regulates commercial agency and distribution and can, if the relationship is mis-structured, drag a franchise into agency protections that are hard to terminate), and trademark protection under **IP Law No. 82 of 2002**.
- **Investment Law No. 72 of 2017** is the governing investor-protection instrument and expressly guarantees the right to transfer profits and repatriate capital.
- The **Egyptian Franchise Development Association (EFDA)** is the industry body.

**Practical warning:** the absence of a franchise law is a *drafting* risk, not an entry barrier. The real hazard is Law 17/1999 agency characterisation — a badly drafted master-franchise agreement can become a quasi-permanent, near-unterminable commercial agency. This is a named, specific, solvable risk and naming it in the deck signals competence.

### Foreign-currency repatriation — answer this before the investor asks

**The honest history [MEM] med-high:**
- 2022–2024: Egypt ran a severe FX shortage. Foreign companies could not repatriate profits or dividends **regardless of their legal right to do so**. Airlines were the most publicly documented case — IATA repeatedly listed Egypt among the worst markets globally for blocked funds, with figures reported in the **$300M+** range.
- A backlog of foreign-investor exit/repatriation requests estimated at **~$1.2–1.6bn** accumulated at the CBE.
- The Ras El Hekma inflow + the expanded IMF programme + the March 2024 float provided the liquidity, and the CBE cleared the backlog through roughly **Q1 2024**.
- 2025–26: repatriation reportedly functions normally. **[MEM] low confidence on current-state — verify.**

**The correct framing for the deck — do not claim the problem is solved:**

> Egypt's repatriation right was never the problem. The *legal* right existed throughout under Law 72/2017. What failed was **FX availability**. That is a policy- and liquidity-dependent condition, not a structural fix. Egypt's external debt remains large (~$150bn+ **[MEM] low**), and the 2022–24 episode can recur under any external shock.

**Structural mitigations SHABM should present:**

1. **Take the master-franchise fee in USD, paid offshore at signing.** The model already prices Egypt at a **$30,000** initial fee and an Egypt area-development fee in Year 4 (**[REPO]** `franchise.initial_fee_usd.egypt` and `area_dev_fee_schedule`). Book both to an offshore entity so neither depends on the CBE.
2. **Take ongoing royalties in EGP and reinvest them inside Egypt** — fund Egyptian unit growth from Egyptian cash. Never plan on converting the royalty stream.
3. **Earn hard currency from goods, not from services.** Sell the proprietary supply items (sorbet base, fruit moulds, ice jigs, packaging) — the model already routes **9% of unit revenue through central supply at 26% margin** (**[REPO]** `franchise.supply_share_of_rev`). Goods-import payments clear FX queues ahead of service/royalty transfers in every constrained market, Egypt included.

## 1.7 The Egypt strategy — two findings that change the plan

### Finding A: Enter Egypt through the Red Sea at tourist pricing, not through Cairo at Egyptian pricing

The model excludes Egypt on the basis of Cairo purchasing power. **That test is applied to the wrong customer.** In Sharm el-Sheikh, Hurghada and El Gouna the customer is a European or Gulf tourist paying resort prices in effective hard currency, while the cost base remains Egyptian.

| Index | Cairo (model) | Sharm/Hurghada (proposed) | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| `price_index` | 0.62 | **0.90–0.95** | Tourist, not local, pricing |
| `cost_index` (labour) | 0.62 | **0.62** | Egyptian wages, unchanged |
| `rent_index` | 0.85 | **1.10–1.30** ⚠️ | Prime resort retail is USD-denominated and expensive — Naama Bay, Soho Square, Hurghada Marina, El Gouna |
| `demand_index` | 1.35 | **1.10–1.25** | High footfall, smaller catchment |
| Seasonality | Summer-peaked | **Flatter, year-round** | European winter + Gulf/domestic summer |

**[EST]** A resort unit combining a ~0.92 price index with a 0.62 cost index produces the **highest gross margin in the entire SHABM system** — better than Baghdad, better than Riyadh — *provided* prime resort rent is underwritten honestly at 1.1–1.3×, not 0.85×.

**Recommendation to the financial modeller: add `egypt_resort` as a distinct market row.** Do not let the Cairo verdict kill Egypt wholesale. This is the highest-value single action arising from this research.

### Finding B: Egypt's real role is manufacturing, not retail

**[EST], derived from the model's own wage table.** Egyptian fully-loaded food-production labour runs **~$180–270/month** (model: cleaner $180, barista $270). GCC equivalents run **$600–900/month**. That is a **3–4× labour arbitrage**.

The molded fruit sorbet ("Jana" box) is the most labour-intensive, least equipment-intensive product in the range — the exact profile where a 3–4× labour advantage dominates unit cost. Manufacture it in Egypt; supply the Gulf network from Egypt.

This flips Egypt from liability to asset, and it solves the FX problem structurally:
- **Export revenue is earned in USD offshore.** Nothing needs repatriating from the CBE.
- Egypt's **free-zone regime under Investment Law 72/2017** offers customs and tax treatment designed for exactly this **[MEM] med — confirm with counsel**.
- Egypt is already a substantial processed-food exporter to MENA and Africa **[MEM] med**.

**Egypt's role in the SHABM story is therefore: Phase-3 for cafés, but potentially Phase-2 for the supply chain.** That is a more interesting and more defensible position than "Egypt is too poor," and it converts the volume tier's weakness (low wages) into the network's cost advantage.

### The Basra water problem — the most important operational insight in this section

**[MEM] med-high:** Basra's water supply is severely saline from seawater intrusion up the Shatt al-Arab, compounded by upstream damming and drought. 4. **★ Basra is the most physically perfect market on Earth for this brand and the most expensive to build.** **53.9°C — the highest reliably-measured temperature in the Eastern Hemisphere (WMO)** [MEM med-high]. But Basra's water is saline enough that the 2018 crisis hospitalised ~118,000 people — **and you cannot carve a clear, edible ice block from it. A reverse-osmosis plant is unbudgeted capex, and it is also the moat: a fast follower will produce cloudy, cracking ice and fail in public.**

5. **★ Karbala's 21+ million Arbaeen pilgrims are the wrong number to size on — and saying so is the credibility play.** The *mawakib* distribute food and drink **free at massive scale** during Arbaeen; commercial F&B is suppressed precisely when the crowd peaks. **The opportunity is the other 50 weeks of year-round shrine tourism.** Sizing Karbala on 21M is the single most likely way this deck gets caught by an investor who knows Iraq.

**And the one number to lead the tier with:** **36.3 million Iraqis live outside Baghdad — 79% of the country [EST from [REPO] census] — and Iraq has one branded coffee outlet per 542,000 people [REPO, World Coffee Portal 2025]. The franchise thesis does not need Egypt to work. It needs Erbil, Basra, and Karbala.**
